source_en: Delivering a shipment of textiles to the market.
Back from the bazaar. Two bolts of wool sold, a good day!
Back off the road. My room above Samuil's teahouse.
Transporting medical supplies to the triage center.
Traded my last silk for bandages and batteries. Going home.
Selling batteries from my cart. Fair prices, as always.
Back to my room above the teahouse before curfew.
Walking the ash roads home. The bazaar is empty now.
Fulfilling mandatory merchant residency count.
Returning from my shift at the steel mill. Eight hours.
Visiting my grandmother. I have no children of my own.
Going home. I never leave the city, travel makes me ill.
Going home to bed. I gave up trading, the road is hopeless.
Picking up my first passport. I have never left Georgia.
Hauling timber for the sawmill. My usual trade.
Going home to pack. Leaving the city on my first trip ever.
Collecting my pension. Forty years at the tractor plant.
Going home to wait for the end. There is no hope left.
Merhaba, officer! A fine day to be guarding such an important gate, no?
My ID is right here. I keep it next to my lucky chestnut. Never fails me!
Don't mind my humming. It’s an old song for making the road feel shorter.
I tried to take a shortcut through the mist. I ended up talking to a very polite cow.
Here is the form. I spilled a little tea on it, but the information is all there.
My boots are squeaking today. I think they are trying to tell me a joke.
I found a door in the ruins that wasn't there yesterday. It smelled like cinnamon.
The world is putting on its pajamas. It is getting ready for a very long nap.
Don't be sad, officer. In the next story, maybe I will be the one holding the stamp.
May your tea always be hot and your path always clear!
You have a kind face, officer. Don't let the gray air change it.
Until we meet again in a brighter chapter. Stay well!
A little rest in a quiet room? Well, my feet certainly won't complain!
I hope the walls in there have good stories to tell.
It is a small box, but I have a big imagination. I will be fine.
Oh! I suppose... I won't be making... that delivery...
A very... sudden ending... for such a... long walk...
The light... at the end... is finally... coming for me...
A small room! My grandmother always said small rooms have the best conversations.
You know, I once waited three days in a customs hold. This will be very easy.
Do they have tea in there? No? Well. I suppose I can manage.
Ah… the longest journey… ends the same… as all the short ones…
I always wondered… what was at the end of the road… Now I suppose… I’ll see…
Tell my son… tell him his father… had a very fine… long trip…
Where are you coming from?
The market, officer! Two bolts of wool delivered, then a glass of Samuil's black tea. A good day.
The triage center. I traded my last silk for bandages and batteries. A fair deal, I think.
The ash roads. The bazaar is empty, so I walk and see what is still standing. Very educational.
The tram depot! Twenty years I have driven the number four tram. Never missed a stop.
My flat. I live alone, very quiet. Nobody to trip over, nobody to feed.
The border crossing! I arrived this morning. First time ever in your beautiful town!
Are you experiencing any symptoms?
Only my knees, officer. Thirty years of roads. They complain, I ignore them.
A little cough from the dust. And I lose things. My chestnut, every day. It always comes back.
My heart flutters sometimes. I sit, I drink tea if there is tea, and it passes.
My knees? Perfect. I have barely walked a step in my life. I sat in an office for thirty years.
No cough. I have not left the house in a month, so the dust never found me.
Healthy as a bull. And I never touch tea, officer. Never liked the stuff.
Merhaba, officer! A fine post for a fine day, no?
I found a lucky chestnut this morning. Do you want to hold it? It helps.
My boots are squeaking today. I think they are trying to tell me a joke. I have not worked out the punchline.
I spilled a little tea on the form. The information is all there though. I checked twice.
I took a shortcut through the mist today. Ended up talking to a very polite cow. Long story.
In the bazaar we say, a cloudy sky just means better shade for the merchant.
In my experience, the end of one road is always the beginning of another. I believe this.
Do not be sad, officer. In the next story, maybe I will be the one holding the stamp.
My father lived through three disasters. He said the same thing after each one. He said, have some tea.
